title: Two lungs
hookLine: John Paul II said the Church must breathe with both lungs, East and West

cards: Take one slow breath, right now, and notice it. Both sides of your chest rise. You don't decide to use the left lung or the right one; they work together, or you work less well.

A pope from Poland, John Paul the Second, reached for exactly this picture when he wrote about Christians of East and West, long apart, and the Church they belong to. Not a ladder, not a building, not an army.
A pair of lungs. Today, two lungs.

teach.b: Across this stretch, this path has met the first Christians and the Fathers, and they came from both halves of the old world: Greek speakers like John Chrysostom and John of Damascus, Latin speakers like Augustine, Leo and Gregory, monks in Egypt, on Athos and at Monte Cassino.

For a long time they belonged to one Church, praying in different languages and styles. Then East and West drifted apart over language, politics and theology, and in the end broke communion with each other.
That wound is still open. Catholics and Orthodox Christians share the sacraments and the apostles, but don't yet share one table.
Pope John Paul the Second wrote, in his letter on Christian unity, that the Church must breathe with her two lungs, East and West.
The Eastern traditions, their icons, their chant, their long liturgies, their monks, aren't decoration on a Latin Church.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: They are half of its breathing. And inside the Catholic Church itself, Eastern Catholic Churches, like the Ukrainian Greek Catholics you met yesterday, already pray in the Eastern way in communion with Rome.
Underneath is an older picture still. In Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, God "breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul."

Breath is a gift before it's an achievement. And unity, for John Paul, was something to pray for, not to force. His letter takes its name from Jesus's prayer in John's Gospel: "That they all may be one."

how: The Catholic Church includes both the Latin Church and Eastern Catholic Churches with their own liturgies, and Catholics pray for unity with the Orthodox, especially in the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

games.q: you're a pope who wants the Church's East and West to come together. which picture do you choose?
o: a strong army with one general.
a ladder with the West on top.
games.why: John Paul chose two lungs: neither one is the boss, and a body needs both to breathe fully.

practice: Put one hand on each side of your chest, breathe in slowly, filling both sides, and let it go; then once more, deeper. Rest your hands and notice both sides working without being asked.
If you pray, let the words from John, that they all may be one, ride the breath; if not, simply rest in breathing.

wordCard.voice: Two lungs. John Paul the Second's picture of the Church breathing with both its traditions, East and West. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: breath — the word the Greek Old Testament uses for the breath of life in Genesis 2:7.
